The Microsoft Hex Editor extension is a good option.

Q: Selenium "ERR_TUNNEL_CONNECTION_FAILED" A:

When inputting your proxy, make sure the proxy is working especially since public free proxies could stop working at any moment. Also make sure to specify which type of proxy you are using within the argument.

For example:

chrome_options.add_argument('--proxy-server='"socks4://"+PROXY)

Q: What are the meanings of Windows service trigger types 7 and 30? A:

winsvc.h lists the following, with no additional documentation:

//
// Service trigger types
//
#define SERVICE_TRIGGER_TYPE_DEVICE_INTERFACE_ARRIVAL               1
#define SERVICE_TRIGGER_TYPE_IP_ADDRESS_AVAILABILITY                2
#define SERVICE_TRIGGER_TYPE_DOMAIN_JOIN                            3
#define SERVICE_TRIGGER_TYPE_FIREWALL_PORT_EVENT                    4
#define SERVICE_TRIGGER_TYPE_GROUP_POLICY                           5
#define SERVICE_TRIGGER_TYPE_NETWORK_ENDPOINT                       6
#define SERVICE_TRIGGER_TYPE_CUSTOM_SYSTEM_STATE_CHANGE             7
#define SERVICE_TRIGGER_TYPE_CUSTOM                                 20
#define SERVICE_TRIGGER_TYPE_AGGREGATE                              30

AI gives some additional information by querying these specific names for 7 and 30, but I'll leave that to you to research.

Q: Applying FUN in ave() to only a subset of the group A:

Some thoughts up front:

  • Rui's answer appears much more readable: you pass in just the columns needed, and calculate a single response, and capture it. It runs once per $A group and gives the desired response. It returns a full frame because the response is replicated across all of the inputs (and some other class-preserving steps).

  • Similarly, we could have just added $B to the end of your code. This is identical in results and time as Rui's answer.

An alternative that appears to be much faster, and without the need to do a post-ave subset:

ave(seq_along(x$B), x$A, FUN=function(i) with(x[i,], mean(B[C < 3])))
# [1] 1.5 1.5 3.5 3.5 3.5

The reason I'm posting this as a standalone answer is I think it deserves a quick mention and benchmark.

bench::mark(
  op  = ave(x, x$A, FUN=function(y) { mean( y$B[y$C < 3] ) })$B, 
  rui = ave(x[c("B", "C")], x$A, FUN = \(b) with(b, mean(B[C < 3])))$B, 
  r2  = ave(seq_along(x$B), x$A, FUN=function(i) with(x[i,], mean(B[C < 3])))
)
# # A tibble: 3 × 13
#   expression      min   median `itr/sec` mem_alloc `gc/sec` n_itr  n_gc total_time result    memory             time               gc                  
#   <bch:expr> <bch:tm> <bch:tm>     <dbl> <bch:byt>    <dbl> <int> <dbl>   <bch:tm> <list>    <list>             <list>             <list>              
# 1 op           92.7µs  106.8µs     8192.        0B     4.14  3954     2      483ms <dbl [5]> <Rprofmem [0 × 3]> <bench_tm [3,956]> <tibble [3,956 × 3]>
# 2 rui          90.9µs     98µs     9843.        0B     7.38  2668     2      271ms <dbl [5]> <Rprofmem [0 × 3]> <bench_tm [2,670]> <tibble [2,670 × 3]>
# 3 r2           62.9µs   70.2µs    14101.        0B     4.13  6833     2      485ms <dbl [5]> <Rprofmem [0 × 3]> <bench_tm [6,835]> <tibble [6,835 × 3]>

I'm not chasing benchmarks, so my advice is thus:

  • If your data is small-ish and the time-to-complete is quite acceptable, I like adding $B to your code the best: it is very readable/maintainable, and if you ever need another variable for internal consideration, it's already available.

  • Subsetting ala Rui's answer is just a little faster, though honestly not enough where I'd consider it a dominant winner. It is a bit more declarative in that you only need those columns.

  • If your data is larger and has a lot of small groups, then my solution is just a little faster. For a dataset with 5000 rows (many groups) instead of just 5, it completes 3x as fast; for 50,000 rows, its savings is much more.

Again, not chasing the benchmark, but if you find you need to speed up your calcs, consider sending the row-indices instead of the data itself.
